title: Impact of Software Change
concept:
Every software change carries the risk of introducing new defects or of revealing latent defects. The CTFL syllabus emphasises understanding the impact of changes as a core skill.

**Sources of change**: defect fixes, new features, refactoring, library updates, infrastructure changes, configuration changes, environment changes. Even seemingly trivial changes (a library minor version bump) can cause regression.

**Impact analysis** is the activity of identifying everything that might be affected by a change. It uses traceability: trace from the changed code/requirement to other code that depends on it, to test cases that exercise it, to other requirements that interact with it.

Good impact analysis answers: which other modules might break? Which test cases need to re-run? Which acceptance criteria might be affected? Which documents (architecture, user manual, training) need updating?

The cost of poor impact analysis is high: missed regressions reach production, customer-facing failures occur, and the team loses trust. Tooling helps: dependency graphs from build systems, requirement traceability matrices, test management tools that show coverage, static analysis that detects affected call chains.
keyPoints: Every change — even a library bump — can introduce regression.
Impact analysis identifies all components, tests, requirements, and documents affected by a change.
Good traceability and tooling (dependency graphs, traceability matrices) make impact analysis tractable at scale.

quiz.question: Which activity helps a team decide which regression tests must be re-run after a code change?
options: Impact analysis using traceability between code, requirements, and tests
quiz.explanation: Impact analysis traces from the changed item to all dependent items — including the test cases that cover them — so the team can choose which regression tests are necessary. Defect triage prioritises defects; acceptance criteria define done; benchmarking measures performance.
